title: Tilly and the Feeling Pebbles
markdown:
Beside a babbling brook sat Mrs. Honey’s Tea Garden. Sunbeams danced through old oaks, dappled patterns on the ground. The air smelled of sweet honey cakes and cheerful flowers. Mrs. Honey’s apron was always dusted with flour, like a soft snowfall. Her smile was as warm as a fresh-baked loaf.

The garden had a happy way of choosing tables. A kind deer with long gentle eyelashes spent his mornings painting numbers on smooth pebbles, berry juice staining his hooves a polite pink. A neat 1 on one, a jolly 2 on another, and so on, each number drying in the sun before anyone could argue with it.

The pebbles were so smooth and nice to hold. Soon visitors stopped looking at the numbers. They would pick up a pebble and feel its weight and texture.

“Oh my,” a lady might say, “this one feels like a quiet whisper on a summer breeze.” And she would sit at the table that pebble seemed to belong to.

“And this one,” a gentleman would smile, “is like a warm hug.”

Tables chosen not by numbers, but by the feeling of the pebbles. A lovely way to find a perfect spot.

Into this sunny garden skipped Tilly the kitten, fur the colour of sunshine. Beside her ambled Ivy the hedgehog, quills a soft rustling sound. Tilly’s bright green eyes were wide.

“Ivy! Look at all those lovely pebbles! Which one should we pick? Which one feels like the bestest place to sit?”

Ivy peered. “They are rather nice. So many different shapes and colours, and they all look so smooth.”

Mrs. Honey came over, kind face beaming, a plate of tiny golden honey biscuits in her hands. “Welcome. Have you decided on your table yet?”

Tilly bounced. “Not yet! But look, the deer painted numbers on them!” She pointed to a pebble with a cheerful 3. “I like number three! It looks like a happy number!”

Ivy was more interested in the pebbles themselves. She nudged one with her nose: small, brown, seeming to absorb the sunlight. “This one feels like a cool smooth river stone that water has tumbled for a long time.”

“But the number is more important,” Tilly insisted. She did peek at a pebble that shimmered, a tiny captured jewel. Very pretty. When she touched it, a little bumpy, a little sharp.

Mrs. Honey chuckled softly. “Many people find that the pebbles themselves will tell them where they’ll be happiest. Just feel them. Let your paws and your hearts decide.”

Tilly looked again at the shimmering jewel pebble, then at the smooth cool one Ivy had nudged. A funny feeling fluttered in her chest. Usually she was first to grab the brightest, shiniest thing. That was her way, and it had always worked for ribbons and sunbeams. The shiny pebble felt a little too much. Pretty, but not quite right for a quiet tea. A bit too loud, as if it wanted a brass band instead of a teapot.

She looked at the smooth grey pebble again. It did not sparkle. It did not have a bright loud number. When she gently picked it up, coolness spread through her paw. A quiet peaceful calm. Just right. A peaceful lazy afternoon, perfect for dreaming.

“I think,” she said softly, surprising even herself, “I will have this one.” She nudged the smooth quiet pebble toward a little table tucked under a blossoming cherry tree.

Ivy smiled, a slow gentle hedgehog smile. “And I will have this one.” A pebble that felt as if it held a warm quiet. Like a snug little burrow, safe and cozy. She placed it carefully beside Tilly’s stone.

They sat at their little table. Cherry blossoms drifted like soft pink confetti onto the biscuits. Soon Mrs. Honey arrived with a tiny teapot and two little cups, warm creamy milk and sweet golden honey. Tilly took a sip. Warm and sweet, just like the quiet comforting feeling of her pebble. From here, under the cherry tree, the garden seemed wonderfully peaceful: the brook still babbled, but it babbled at a polite distance, and the numbered pebbles on other tables kept their own company.

“You know, Ivy,” green eyes soft, “this pebble isn’t sparkly or very colourful, but it feels very, very happy. It feels like a good place to be.”

Ivy nodded. “And mine feels like a warm blanket on a sleepy afternoon. Funny. The number wasn’t important at all. The feeling was.”

The next day, when Mrs. Honey brought out a new batch, one pebble was as shiny and sparkly as a disco ball. Tilly looked at it for just a second. Then, with a happy little purr, she nudged the quiet smooth stone beside it, and smiled. Listening to her own quiet feelings, to what felt truly right in heart and paws, could lead to the most delightful peaceful places.

She logged jewel-pebble / cool-grey / cherry-table beside the cups, left the disco-ball shine for someone who wanted loud, and let Ivy keep the burrow-warm stone while the honey-sweet milk lasted. Their tummies full, they finished their tea, the smooth comforting pebbles resting beside the little cups.
